original: ROSS. From Fife, great King, Where the Norweyan banners flout the sky And fan our people cold. Norway himself, with terrible numbers, Assisted by that most disloyal traitor, The Thane of Cawdor, began a dismal conflict; Till that Bellona’s bridegroom, lapp’d in proof, Confronted him with self-comparisons, Point against point, rebellious arm ’gainst arm, Curbing his lavish spirit: and, to conclude, The victory fell on us.
before: ROSS. From Fife, great King, where the Norwegian banners taunt the sky and chill our people with fear. Norway himself, with terrible numbers, aided by that most disloyal traitor the Thane of Cawdor, began a grim battle. But Macbeth, like the god of war's own champion, clad in proven armor, met the Norwegian blow for blow, sword against sword, curbing his wild aggression. And to make a long story short, the victory fell to us.
after: ROSS. From Fife, great King, where the Norwegian banners taunt the sky and chill our people with fear. Norway himself, with terrible numbers, aided by that most disloyal traitor the Thane of Cawdor, began a grim battle. But Macbeth, like the bridegroom of Bellona, goddess of war, clad in proven armor, met the Norwegian blow for blow, sword against sword, curbing his wild aggression. And to make a long story short, the victory fell to us.

original: ROSS. That now Sweno, the Norways’ king, craves composition; Nor would we deign him burial of his men Till he disbursed at Saint Colme’s Inch Ten thousand dollars to our general use.
before: ROSS. And now Sweno, the King of Norway, begs for a peace treaty. We wouldn't even let him bury his dead until he paid us ten thousand dollars at Saint Colme's Inch for our general use.
after: ROSS. And now Sweno, the King of Norway, begs for a peace treaty. We wouldn't even let him bury his dead until he paid us ten thousand silver dollars at Saint Colme's Inch for our general use.

original: MACBETH. Stay, you imperfect speakers, tell me more. By Sinel’s death I know I am Thane of Glamis; But how of Cawdor? The Thane of Cawdor lives, A prosperous gentleman; and to be king Stands not within the prospect of belief, No more than to be Cawdor. Say from whence You owe this strange intelligence? or why Upon this blasted heath you stop our way With such prophetic greeting?—Speak, I charge you.
before: MACBETH. Wait, you incomplete prophets, tell me more. Through my father Sinel's death, I know I am Thane of Glamis. But how can I be Thane of Cawdor? The Thane of Cawdor is alive and thriving. And to be king is no more within the realm of possibility than to be Cawdor. Tell me where you got this strange knowledge, or why you stop us on this desolate heath with such a prophetic greeting. Speak, I command you.
after: MACBETH. Wait, you who tell only half the story, tell me more. Through my father Sinel's death, I know I am Thane of Glamis. But how can I be Thane of Cawdor? The Thane of Cawdor is alive and thriving. And to be king is no more within the realm of possibility than to be Cawdor. Tell me where you got this strange knowledge, or why you stop us on this desolate heath with such a prophetic greeting. Speak, I command you.

original: DUNCAN. Welcome hither: I have begun to plant thee, and will labour To make thee full of growing.—Noble Banquo, That hast no less deserv’d, nor must be known No less to have done so, let me infold thee And hold thee to my heart.
before: DUNCAN. Welcome! I have begun to invest in you, and I will work to see you flourish. Noble Banquo, you have deserved no less, and must be recognized no less for having done so. Let me embrace you and hold you to my heart.
after: DUNCAN. Welcome! I’ve planted you, and I’ll help you grow. Noble Banquo, you have deserved no less, and must be recognized no less for having done so. Let me embrace you and hold you to my heart.

original: MACBETH. Whence is that knocking? How is’t with me, when every noise appals me? What hands are here? Ha, they pluck out mine eyes! Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather The multitudinous seas incarnadine, Making the green one red.
before: MACBETH. Where is that knocking coming from? What is happening to me, when every noise terrifies me? What hands are these? They're plucking out my eyes! Will all the water in the ocean wash this blood clean from my hands? No. These hands of mine would sooner turn the countless seas red, making the green ocean entirely crimson.
after: MACBETH. Where is that knocking coming from? What is happening to me, when every noise terrifies me? What hands are these? They're plucking out my eyes! Will all the water in great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood clean from my hands? No. These hands of mine would sooner turn the countless seas red, making the green ocean entirely crimson.

original: PORTER. Here’s a knocking indeed! If a man were porter of hell gate, he should have old turning the key. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock. Who’s there, i’ th’ name of Belzebub? Here’s a farmer that hanged himself on the expectation of plenty: come in time; have napkins enow about you; here you’ll sweat for’t. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock! Who’s there, i’ th’ other devil’s name? Faith, here’s an equivocator, that could swear in both the scales against either scale, who committed treason enough for God’s sake, yet could not equivocate to heaven: O, come in, equivocator. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock! Who’s there? Faith, here’s an English tailor come hither, for stealing out of a French hose: come in, tailor; here you may roast your goose. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock. Never at quiet! What are you?—But this place is too cold for hell. I’ll devil-porter it no further: I had thought to have let in some of all professions, that go the primrose way to th’ everlasting bonfire. [_Knocking._] Anon, anon! I pray you, remember the porter.
before: PORTER. There's some knocking indeed! If a man were the porter of hell's gate, he'd get tired of turning the key. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock! Who's there, in the name of the devil? Here's a farmer who hanged himself because he expected prices to drop after a good harvest. Come right in! Better bring plenty of handkerchiefs; you'll sweat in here. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock! Who's there, in the other devil's name? Well now, here's a smooth-talking liar who could swear on both sides of any argument, who committed plenty of treason for God's sake but couldn't talk his way into heaven. Come in, you equivocator! [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock! Who's there? Here's an English tailor who's been sent here for skimping on cloth while making French-style trousers. Come in, tailor; here you can heat your pressing iron. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock! Never a moment's peace! Who are you? But this place is too cold for hell. I'll stop playing hell's doorman. I had intended to let in someone from every profession that takes the flowery path to the everlasting bonfire. [_Knocking._] All right, all right! Coming! Please, remember to tip the porter.
after: PORTER. There's some knocking indeed! If a man were the porter of hell's gate, he'd get tired of turning the key. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock! Who's there, in Beelzebub’s name? Here's a farmer who hanged himself because he expected prices to drop after a good harvest. Come right in! Better bring plenty of handkerchiefs; you'll sweat in here. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock! Who's there, in the other devil's name? Well now, here's a smooth-talking liar who could swear on both sides of any argument, who committed plenty of treason for God's sake but couldn't talk his way into heaven. Come in, you equivocator! [_Knocking._] Knock, knock, knock! Who's there? Here's an English tailor who's been sent here for skimping on cloth while making French-style trousers. Come in, tailor; here you can roast your goose of a pressing iron. [_Knocking._] Knock, knock! Never a moment's peace! Who are you? But this place is too cold for hell. I'll stop playing hell's doorman. I had intended to let in someone from every profession that takes the flowery path to the everlasting bonfire. [_Knocking._] All right, all right! Coming! Please, remember to tip the porter.

original: PORTER. Marry, sir, nose-painting, sleep, and urine. Lechery, sir, it provokes and unprovokes; it provokes the desire, but it takes away the performance. Therefore much drink may be said to be an equivocator with lechery: it makes him, and it mars him; it sets him on, and it takes him off; it persuades him, and disheartens him; makes him stand to, and not stand to; in conclusion, equivocates him in a sleep, and giving him the lie, leaves him.
before: PORTER. Well, sir: a red nose, sleep, and urination. As for lust, sir, it both encourages and discourages it. It creates the desire but takes away the ability. So heavy drinking could be called a double-dealer when it comes to lust: it builds a man up and tears him down; it eggs him on and holds him back; it persuades him and then defeats him; it props him up and then lets him down. In short, it cheats him into a stupor, and having lied to him, leaves him flat.
after: PORTER. Well, sir: a red nose, sleep, and urination. As for lust, sir, it both encourages and discourages it. It creates the desire but takes away the ability. So heavy drinking could be called a double-dealer when it comes to lust: it builds a man up and tears him down; it eggs him on and holds him back; it persuades him and then defeats him; it gets him up and then he can’t keep it up. In short, it cheats him into a stupor, and having lied to him, leaves him flat.

original: MACDUFF. I believe drink gave thee the lie last night.
before: MACDUFF. I think drink got the better of you last night.
after: MACDUFF. I think drink called you a liar and laid you flat last night.

original: PORTER. That it did, sir, i’ the very throat on me; but I requited him for his lie; and (I think) being too strong for him, though he took up my legs sometime, yet I made a shift to cast him.
before: PORTER. That it did, sir, it had me by the throat. But I gave as good as I got. And though it knocked my legs out from under me a few times, I managed to throw it off in the end.
after: PORTER. That it did, sir, it had me by the throat. But I gave as good as I got. And though it knocked my legs out from under me a few times, I managed to throw it up in the end.

original: LORD. He did: and with an absolute “Sir, not I,” The cloudy messenger turns me his back, And hums, as who should say, “You’ll rue the time That clogs me with this answer.”
before: LORD. He did, and when the messenger received an absolute refusal, the man turned his back on the surly messenger with a disapproving hum, as if to say, "You'll regret the day you gave me this answer."
after: LORD. He did. When Macduff gave him a flat “No, sir, not I,” the messenger turned his back with a scowl and a hum, as if to say, “You’ll regret loading me with that answer.”

original: THIRD WITCH. Harpier cries:—’Tis time, ’tis time.
before: THIRD WITCH. My familiar spirit cries: it's time, it's time!
after: THIRD WITCH. Harpier, my familiar spirit, cries: it's time, it's time!

original: FIRST WITCH. Round about the cauldron go; In the poison’d entrails throw.— Toad, that under cold stone Days and nights has thirty-one Swelter’d venom sleeping got, Boil thou first i’ th’ charmed pot!
before: FIRST WITCH. Round about the cauldron go. Into the poisoned brew throw a toad that under a cold stone for thirty-one days and nights has sweated out its venom while sleeping. You boil first in the charmed pot!
after: FIRST WITCH. Circle the cauldron. Throw the poisoned entrails in. Toad that slept beneath a cold stone for thirty-one days and nights, sweating venom: boil first in our enchanted pot!

original: THIRD WITCH. Scale of dragon, tooth of wolf, Witch’s mummy, maw and gulf Of the ravin’d salt-sea shark, Root of hemlock digg’d i’ th’ dark, Liver of blaspheming Jew, Gall of goat, and slips of yew Sliver’d in the moon’s eclipse, Nose of Turk, and Tartar’s lips, Finger of birth-strangled babe Ditch-deliver’d by a drab, Make the gruel thick and slab: Add thereto a tiger’s chaudron, For th’ ingredients of our cauldron.
before: THIRD WITCH. Scale of dragon, tooth of wolf, dried flesh of a witch, stomach and gullet of a ravenous shark from the salt sea, root of hemlock dug up in the dark, liver of a blasphemer, gall of goat, and slips of yew cut during an eclipse of the moon, nose of a Turk, and a Tartar's lips, finger of an infant strangled at birth and delivered in a ditch by a prostitute. Make the gruel thick and slimy. Add to it a tiger's guts, for the ingredients of our cauldron.
after: THIRD WITCH. Scale of dragon, tooth of wolf, dried flesh of a witch, stomach and gullet of a ravenous shark from the salt sea, root of hemlock dug up in the dark, liver of a blaspheming Jew, gall of goat, and slips of yew cut during an eclipse of the moon, nose of a Turk, and a Tartar's lips, finger of an infant strangled at birth and delivered in a ditch by a prostitute. Make the gruel thick and slimy. Add to it a tiger's guts, for the ingredients of our cauldron.

original: MALCOLM. ’Tis call’d the evil: A most miraculous work in this good king; Which often, since my here-remain in England, I have seen him do. How he solicits heaven, Himself best knows, but strangely-visited people, All swoln and ulcerous, pitiful to the eye, The mere despair of surgery, he cures; Hanging a golden stamp about their necks, Put on with holy prayers: and ’tis spoken, To the succeeding royalty he leaves The healing benediction. With this strange virtue, He hath a heavenly gift of prophecy; And sundry blessings hang about his throne, That speak him full of grace.
before: MALCOLM. It's called the King's Evil, a most miraculous power in this good king. Since I've been staying in England, I've seen him do it often. How he appeals to heaven, he himself knows best, but strangely afflicted people, all swollen and covered with sores, pitiful to look at, beyond the hope of surgery, he cures by hanging a golden coin around their necks, placed there with holy prayers. And it's said that he passes this healing gift down to the kings who follow him. Along with this strange power, he has a heavenly gift of prophecy, and many blessings surround his throne that declare him full of grace.
after: MALCOLM. The disease is called the King’s Evil. This good king works a remarkable cure. Since I've been staying in England, I've seen him do it often. How he appeals to heaven, he himself knows best, but strangely afflicted people, all swollen and covered with sores, pitiful to look at, beyond the hope of surgery, he cures by hanging a golden coin around their necks, placed there with holy prayers. And it's said that he passes this healing gift down to the kings who follow him. Along with this strange power, he has a heavenly gift of prophecy, and many blessings surround his throne that declare him full of grace.

original: MACBETH. Throw physic to the dogs, I’ll none of it. Come, put mine armour on; give me my staff: Seyton, send out.—Doctor, the Thanes fly from me.— Come, sir, despatch.—If thou couldst, doctor, cast The water of my land, find her disease, And purge it to a sound and pristine health, I would applaud thee to the very echo, That should applaud again.—Pull’t off, I say.— What rhubarb, senna, or what purgative drug, Would scour these English hence? Hear’st thou of them?
before: MACBETH. Throw medicine to the dogs then; I'll have none of it. Come, put on my armor. Give me my staff. Seyton, send out the riders. Doctor, the thanes are deserting me. Come, sir, hurry. If you could, Doctor, diagnose the disease of my country, find what ails it, and purge it back to sound and pure health, I would applaud you until the echo applauded in return. Pull it off, I say. What drug, what laxative, what purge would flush these English out of here? Have you heard anything about them?
after: MACBETH. Throw medicine to the dogs then; I'll have none of it. Come, put on my armor. Give me my staff. Seyton, send out the riders. Doctor, the thanes are deserting me. Come, sir, hurry. If you could, Doctor, examine my country’s urine, find what ails it, and purge it back to sound and pure health, I would applaud you until the echo applauded in return. Pull it off, I say. What rhubarb, what senna, what purging drug would flush these English out of here? Have you heard anything about them?

original: MACDUFF. Despair thy charm; And let the angel whom thou still hast serv’d Tell thee, Macduff was from his mother’s womb Untimely ripp’d.
before: MACDUFF. Then abandon your charm and know this: Macduff was ripped from his mother's womb before his time. He was not born in the natural way.
after: MACDUFF. Then give up hope in your charm. Let the spirit you’ve served all along tell you this: Macduff was ripped from his mother’s womb before his time.
